raw_response:
I am a 55-year-old farmer in Quzhou County, Hebei Province, China. I have been farming for 30 years and have a middle school education. My farm is 13.1 mu, and I grow wheat and maize in a double-cropping system. My household has 2 people, and I have access to well irrigation. It is the start of the growing season (early October).

---

**My thinking for this year:**

Well, it's October again. I've been doing this wheat-maize rotation for thirty years now, so I know the drill. My wife and I are getting older, and with just the two of us, labor is tight during the busy seasons — especially that week between wheat harvest and maize planting in June. I can't afford to mess up the timing.

For the **winter wheat**, I'll plant the whole 13.1 mu. I'm sticking with the improved variety I've used for the past few years — the seed shop says it's high-yielding, and last year I got about 450 jin per mu, which was decent. I don't buy the most expensive hybrid seeds; the mid-range ones work fine and save me some money. I'll put the seed down in the first week of October, right after I've turned the soil. The extension agent told us that 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is about right, but honestly, I usually do a bit more because I'm worried about a cold winter hurting the tillering. I'll put down a base of compound fertilizer before planting — about 50 jin of 15-15-15 per mu — and then topdress with urea at green-up time in spring, maybe another 30 jin per mu. That brings my nitrogen to around 17-18 kg per mu. I know it's a bit high, but I'd rather waste a little fertilizer than risk a bad yield. My neighbor, Old Wang, cut back last year and his wheat was yellow at jointing — I don't want that.

For irrigation, I'll water three times: once before winter to help the seedlings establish, once at jointing in March or April, and once at grain filling in May. The pumping costs about 40 yuan per mu each time, so that's 120 yuan per mu just for water, but you can't skip it. The well water is metered now and getting expensive, but what can you do? I'll spray a herbicide after planting to keep the weeds down, and maybe a fungicide in spring if I see rust — it was bad two years ago.

For **summer maize**, the whole 13.1 mu goes into maize right after wheat harvest in early June. The turnaround is brutal — sometimes only five or six days. I hire a combine for wheat harvest, and then I need to get the maize in fast. I'll buy hybrid maize seed; it's non-negotiable for maize, about 3 jin per mu. I plant around mid-June, as soon as the wheat is off. Fertilizer for maize: another 50 jin of compound fertilizer at planting, and I'll side-dress urea at the big trumpet stage if the rains are good — maybe 25 jin per mu. That gives me about 15 kg N per mu total for maize. I used to do more, but maize responds less to extra fertilizer than wheat does, and the price of urea went up last year.

Maize irrigation depends on the rains. If July and August are normal, maybe I only water once at flowering. If it's dry like 2022, I'll water twice. I'll budget for two times to be safe. I'll spray herbicide and maybe insecticide if there are armyworms — I've seen them in the area.

For labor, my wife and I do most of the work, but during harvest and planting I hire 4-5 days of labor at 150 yuan per day. It's a cost, but two people can't handle 13 mu of harvest alone anymore, not at our age.

Total input costs this year will be around 8,000 to 8,500 yuan. That's a big chunk of our savings, but if wheat yields 450 kg/mu and maize yields 500 kg/mu, and prices hold, we should make a decent profit. I'm not changing much from last year — at my age, with only 13 mu, stability matters more than experimenting.
